title: Crisis team saved one man, another not so lucky
article: Two deranged men -- one armed with a gun, one armed with a knife - - confronted Toronto police this past weekend in two separate incidents, one died, the other lived.
Want to guess who was shot to death by police?
If you guessed the man with a gun, the man most capable of harming or killing the largest number of people, you'd be dead wrong.

O'brien Christopher\-Reid, a 26-year-old Toronto man, was shot to death Sunday afternoon in Edwards Gardens -- the number one wedding photo location in Toronto -- while police were trying to arrest him. They'd rushed into the park after receiving reports of a half-naked man with a large knife. It appears three officers fired their guns, and one was slightly wounded by a bullet fragment, according to the province's Special Investigations Unit, which is probing Christopher- Reid's death.

Just 14 hours earlier, police safely arrested an "emotionally disturbed" 29-year-old North York man who allegedly choked his eight- months pregnant wife, followed her to the local police station and fired two shots at her as she turned into the police parking lot.

After a chase through several kilometres of residential streets, the man was boxed in by officers, who kept him contained for an hour until the Emergency Task Force assumed control of the scene. Thirty minutes later, they convinced the armed man to give himself up.
One dies, one lives -- what gives?

I'm not being flippant. The tragic end to one incident and the success of the other police intervention raises serious and crucial questions about the training and tools at the disposal of police here -- and in other cities.

In the past two decades, more than two dozen men have been shot and killed (or very seriously injured) by police here -- most of them were non-white, most of them were mentally ill or otherwise incapacitated. While much public anger has focussed on the race issue -- and may very well again in Christopher-Reid's case -- inquest juries have returned again and again to issues of mental health care, the poor state of police training, and the inadequate collection of non-lethal tools at their disposal.

Much has changed in those two decades -- all officers receive mandatory training in dealing with the mentally ill now, protocol calls for the Emergency Task Force to be called when dealing with disturbed suspects, and a special crisis intervention team (modeled after the Hamilton police COAST program which pairs social workers with specially trained officers) has been put in place.
Unfortunately the crisis intervention team only works weekdays. And the ETF takes anywhere from 20-60 minutes to suit up, assemble, and take total charge of a scene. Which leaves the training.

Detective Gino Pulla took part in the successful -- safe -- arrest of the gun-wielding 29-year old man. He says their training, combined with the mandatory debriefing they conduct following every gun call, stood them in good stead. There is a publication ban on details of the case, but Pulla walked through the incident for me, and praised a patrol officer, Mark Little, who hid behind a tree very close to where the gunman sat in his shiny SUV, and opened up lines of communication.

"He called out to him, kept him talking. You keep him talking and the adrenaline goes down ... he did a bang-up job." Little kept the man, who claimed to be deranged by cocaine, occupied and stable until the ETF took over about an hour after the patrol cars had boxed the man in on the residential suburban street.

"It couldn't have gone better than that: no police officer was hurt, no civilians were hurt and no bad guy was hurt -- everybody got to go home safe. Well, except one guy didn't get to go home, but we'll find a place for him."
In stark contrast, according to the SIU, the three patrol officers tried to arrest, not contain, Christopher-Reid, who was armed with a knife, not a gun. The only place for him now is in a grave.
Do police take greater chances with a deranged knife-wielding man than they do with an disturbed man armed with a gun?

Lawyer Julian Falconer -- in Hamilton on a civil trial -- had to collect his thoughts to remember how many families of police shooting victims he's represented at inquests (at least three in the past decade). He said he doesn't know if the weapon, or police attitudes to it, make a real difference in these cases.

"It's truly depressing to think of the number of times we've visited this issue," Falconer said. Falconer says the same answers come up every time -- and crisis team intervention, like Hamilton's COAST program, is one of the keys. Well-trained teams can defuse a situation before someone has to be shot.
"Chief Fantino has consistently sought money for enforcement initiatives, helicopters and the like, but the question is, how much is going into community policing, which is what crisis team are?
"It's our position that there have been insufficient resources put into crisis team interventions," Falconer said.
"People will continue to die in circumstances where their lives might have been saved" until that changes, he said.
